scenes.title: Hulls in the Fog
scenes.text:
The fog came off the estuary in the hour before dawn and lay on the Long Quay like wet wool, and Tamsin Orrey counted hulls by the sound of them.

You could do it, if you had done it long enough. A salt-barge on the mud at low water made a different noise from a coaster: a deep, patient creak, timbers settling against their own weight, where a coaster ticked and dripped like a clock running down. Three years of low-tide counts had taught her the difference. Old Faraday, who had trained her, claimed he could tell a ship's home port by the way its rigging sang. Tamsin did not believe him, but she had never caught him out either.

She walked the edge of the quay with her slate under her arm and her lantern held low, so the light fell on the mud and not back into her eyes. Every few yards she stopped, found a hull with the lantern, found the painted name on its bow, and chalked it. Eleven so far. The *Marigold*, the *Constance*, the *Third Daughter*, two Guild barges with their names freshly gilded and their decks heaped with tarpaulins. The cold got into her left hand, her chalk hand, and she flexed it inside the glove and kept going.

"You'll fall in one day," said a voice below her, "and I'll be the one who has to fish you out."

She lowered the lantern. A flat-bottomed lighter had come up the channel without her hearing it, which meant whoever was poling it knew the mud better than she knew the hulls. The man at the pole was tall and bareheaded, his hair plastered to his skull with fog, and he stood with his weight on his good leg the way he had since he was fifteen.

"Corin Dask," she said. "You're on the wrong side of the quay. The lighter berths are at the Stair."

"I know where the lighter berths are." He shipped the pole and the boat drifted the last yard and bumped against the stones. "I came to find you. They said at the Exchequer you'd be on the count."

"Who said?"

"The porter. Fat man. Smells of cloves."

"Hobb." She crouched at the edge so they were nearer of a height. Close to, he looked worse than the fog accounted for. There were dark half-moons under his eyes, and the knuckles of his right hand were split. "What happened to you?"

"I've been out past the Teeth."

Tamsin said nothing for a moment. The Teeth were the line of rocks across the mouth of the estuary, three miles out, where the bar shoaled and the current turned and ships that misjudged the tide went down without anyone on shore hearing a thing. Nobody went out past the Teeth in a lighter. Lighters were for the harbour. They were barely for the harbour.

"Why," she said.

"There's a wreck there. You'll know it. The *Gannet*, out of Breme." He reached into the front of his coat and took out a packet wrapped in oilskin, the oilskin black and slick and tied around with tarred twine. "She went down at the dark of last moon. A month gone. Ruth Bessaly was her master. You remember Ruth? She used to give us oranges, on the Stair, when her ship came in."

"I remember." She had been nine. Bessaly had been a broad red woman with a voice like a foghorn and a gold tooth she let children touch for luck. "She drowned?"

"All hands, they say. Nobody's found anyone." He held out the packet. "The stern's out of the water at the lowest springs. I went out at slack last night and got into her cabin. This was nailed under the chart table. Nailed, Tam. Somebody wanted it found by somebody who knew where to look."

She took it. The oilskin was cold and heavier than she expected. Through it she could feel the stiff edges of folded paper, and a round hard lump that was probably a seal.

"And you brought it to me," she said, "because—"

"Because it's addressed, and I can read that much, and I can't read the rest." He looked at her. "And because you're the only person I know who works in a building with a roof."

She turned the packet over. Someone had written on the outside of the oilskin in tar, in big careful letters: TO THE LAMP. BY HAND.

"What lamp?"

"I've an idea," Corin said. "But I wanted you to look first. You're the clever one."

"I'm the one with a job to do," she said, but she put the packet inside her coat, against her ribs, where it lay cold and flat. "I've nine more hulls to count and then I'm due at the Ledger Hall. Come and find me tonight."

"Where?"

"Wherever you're tied up."

"The *Patience* is at the Quarter. Same as ever." He picked up his pole. "Tam. Don't show it to anyone at your Exchequer."

"Why not?"

But he had already pushed off, and the fog closed over the lighter, and the last she saw of him was the pale shape of his hands on the pole, going away down the channel toward the Drowned Quarter.

She finished the count. Twenty hulls on the mud on the morning of the third of Thawmonth, and every one of them she could name. She stood for a while at the end of the quay, where the fog was beginning to thin and the first grey light showed the shape of the Exchequer roof on the hill above the town, and she thought about Ruth Bessaly's gold tooth, and the dark of last moon, and the cold weight inside her coat.

Then she went up the hill to work.

scenes.title: The Register
scenes.text:
The Ledger Hall of the Harbour Exchequer was the largest room Tamsin had ever been inside, and she had never once been warm in it.

It ran the whole length of the building's upper floor, under a roof of black beams so high that the lamps hung from them on chains that swung in the draughts. Forty clerks sat at two rows of high desks. The fire at the far end was lit every morning at seven and was for the Chief Assessor's office, which opened off the hall through a glass door, and none of its heat had ever been known to reach the desks.

She hung her wet coat on its hook, with the oilskin packet still inside it, and then went back and took the packet out and put it in the inside pocket of her waistcoat instead, where it made an awkward square bulge she covered with her shawl. Then she sat down, copied her count from the slate into the day-book, and went to the registers.

The hull register for the current quarter stood on its own lectern by the window. It was a great thing, bound in green leather, its pages ruled in red, and every ship that crossed the bar into Quell and paid duty to the Crown was entered in it: name, master, home port, tonnage, cargo, duty paid and the date. The entries were made by the assessors in the Chief Assessor's office and stamped with the Chief Assessor's mark. Junior clerks did not make entries. Junior clerks were allowed to read them.

Tamsin read.

She went back four weeks first, to the dark of last moon, and found the *Gannet* where she expected to find her. Gannet, Breme, master R. Bessaly, sixty tons, salt in bulk, duty paid on forty tons, entered on the second of Rimefall. Outbound for the north coast that same tide. That was the last voyage. That was the voyage she had never come back from.

Then, because she was thorough, and because Faraday had told her once that the only way to read a register was all the way to the end, she kept turning.

The *Gannet* was there again on the twenty-fifth of Rimefall. Eight days ago. Gannet, Breme, master R. Bessaly, sixty tons, salt in bulk, duty paid on forty tons. Inbound. And beside it, in the margin, the round red stamp of the Chief Assessor's mark, an anchor inside a ring.

She read it three times. She put her finger on the line, as though the ink might come away on it. Then she looked up and down the page for any sign of a correction, a crossing out, a note in the margin saying *entered in error*, and there was nothing. The entry was in the same neat round hand as the entries above and below it. It was a perfectly ordinary entry. It said that a ship which had been lying on the rocks past the Teeth for a month, with its master drowned and its cabin full of seawater, had come up the estuary on the flood a week ago and paid its duty like an honest ship.

"Something interesting, Miss Orrey?"

She did not jump, though she wanted to. Edric Vane had a way of arriving beside you that made you feel you had been caught at something even when you had not. He was a tall, soft-spoken man in his fifties, with grey hair worn long over his collar and gold spectacles he took off whenever he wanted to look at you properly. He took them off now.

"The *Gannet*, sir," she said. "Out of Breme. She's entered inbound eight days ago."

"Is she." He did not look at the register. He looked at her.

"She sank, sir. A month ago. Out past the Teeth. Her master drowned."

"Who told you that?"

She hesitated. "It's known on the Stair, sir. The lightermen know."

"The lightermen." Vane smiled. He had a good smile, kind and a little tired, the smile of a man who had explained the same thing to a great many junior clerks. "Miss Orrey, do you know what a lighterman is paid for a wreck?"

"A bounty, sir. A tenth of the salvage."

"A tenth of the salvage, if the wreck is declared. So a lighterman has every reason in the world to find wrecks where there are none, and to tell clerks about them, and to hope that clerks will tell the Exchequer." He put his spectacles back on and finally glanced at the page. "The *Gannet* came in on the twenty-fifth. I remember her. I stamped her myself. Bessaly was in a foul temper about the fog."

"Sir, with respect, I—"

"Miss Orrey." Gently. "The register is the register. It is not a newsletter. It does not record what the lightermen say on the Stair. It records what came across the bar and what was paid. If the *Gannet* went down after the twenty-fifth, then I am very sorry for Captain Bessaly, and no doubt the Guild will file for the rebate in due course, and we'll see it then." He closed the register, quite softly, with one hand. "You have your count to finish."

"I've finished it, sir."

"Then you have the Sorrel assessment to deliver this afternoon. Mother Agathe expects it by four. Don't keep her waiting; she's not a patient woman, and she's not a woman I like to have impatient with this office." He patted her shoulder once, lightly, and went back through the glass door into his warm room.

Tamsin went back to her desk. She sat for a long time with her pen in her hand and did not write anything. The packet against her ribs had warmed to the heat of her body, and she could feel the round lump of the seal through her waistcoat whenever she breathed.

He had not asked who the lighterman was. She noticed that later, on the stairs, with the Sorrel assessment in its folder under her arm. He had asked who told her, and she had said the Stair, and he had let it go. A careful man, a man who stamped every page himself and remembered the weather on the day, and he had not asked which lighterman.

Perhaps because he did not need to.

scenes.title: Assessment at Sorrel House
scenes.text:
It began to rain as she crossed the Saltmarket, a thin cold rain coming in sideways off the water, and by the time she reached Guild Row the hem of her skirt was black to the knee.

Sorrel House stood at the top of the Row where the street widened into a little square with a dry fountain in it. It was the oldest of the Guild houses and the only one still built of timber, black oak beams and white plaster, three storeys leaning out over the street so that the upper windows nearly touched the house across the way. People said the Sorrels had refused to rebuild in stone after the Great Flood because stone was for people who meant to leave. Tamsin had always thought that a strange thing to be proud of, but then she had never understood the Guild.

A manservant took her coat and the folder and showed her up to a room on the first floor that smelled of beeswax and peat smoke. The windows were small and leaded and let in almost nothing of the grey afternoon. There was a fire, at least. There was a fire, and in front of it, in a high-backed chair with a rug over her knees, was Mother Agathe Sorrel.

She was a small woman, much smaller than Tamsin remembered from the Guild processions, and very old. Her hair was white and pulled back so tight it seemed to stretch the skin of her forehead. She wore black, as Guild mothers did, and on every finger of both hands she wore a ring, heavy old rings of gold and jet and green stone that clicked against each other when she moved. Her left eye was clouded milk-white. The right one was dark and quick and missed nothing.

"The Exchequer's girl," she said. "Sit down. You're dripping on my floor."

Tamsin sat on the stool she was pointed to. The manservant brought the folder and gave it to Mother Agathe, who did not open it.

"The quarter's assessment, Mother," Tamsin said. "The Chief Assessor sends his compliments. The Guild's hull duty for the quarter comes to four hundred and twelve crowns, less the rebates already allowed—"

"I can read, child. I've been reading Exchequer assessments since before your mother was born." Agathe laid the folder on her knees and put one ringed hand flat on top of it. "What is your name?"

"Orrey, Mother. Tamsin Orrey."

"Orrey. From the Quarter."

"Yes, Mother."

"Your father was a lighterman."

"Yes."

"Drowned, wasn't he? In the year of the bad ice."

"Yes, Mother." Tamsin kept her voice level. She was not sure what was happening, but she was sure that something was.

"It's a hard trade," Agathe said. "The water takes what it's owed. My husband used to say that the sea keeps a ledger like any other merchant, and it always collects." The dark eye moved over Tamsin's face, unhurried. "I hear you've been asking about the *Gannet*."

The fire cracked. Somewhere below them in the house a door closed.

"I noticed an entry in the register, Mother," Tamsin said carefully. "I mentioned it to the Chief Assessor. It was nothing."

"Was it?"

"He said it was nothing."

"Then I expect it was." Agathe smiled. Her teeth were small and brown and very even. "Edric is a sound man. He's been a good friend to this house for twenty years. If he tells you a thing is nothing, child, you may rest your head on it." She tapped the folder. "Four hundred and twelve, you say."

"Less rebates, Mother."

"Less rebates." She turned her head toward the door. "Iska. See Miss Orrey out. And give her something hot before she goes, she's wet through. We don't want the Exchequer saying we send its clerks home to catch their deaths."

Tamsin had not seen anyone else in the room. But a young woman stood up from the window seat at the far end, where the shadows were deepest, and came forward. She was perhaps twenty-two, tall, with her mother's dark eyes, both of them clear, and a long plain face that might have been handsome if she had not looked so tired. She wore the black of the Guild, but she wore it badly, with ink on the cuffs.

"Come on," she said to Tamsin. "Kitchen's warmest."

They went down two flights of narrow stairs. Iska Sorrel did not speak on the way, and did not take her to the kitchen. She took her to the side door, where the manservant was waiting with Tamsin's coat, and she took the coat from him and sent him away and held it out herself.

"You're not getting anything hot," she said quietly, "you're getting out of this house. My mother likes you."

"That's good, isn't it?"

"No." Iska looked at the door the manservant had gone through, and then back at Tamsin. Up close her face was very young and very serious. "I'll say this once. Don't go out to the Flats on your own. Whatever you think you've found, don't go and look at it on your own."

"I wasn't going to go to the Flats."

"Then good." Iska opened the door. The rain was coming down hard now, hammering on the cobbles of the little square, filling the dry fountain. "Go home, Miss Orrey."

Tamsin went out into the rain. When she turned at the corner of the square to look back, the side door was shut and there was a light in the window seat on the first floor, and a shape in it, very small and very still.

scenes.title: The Patience
scenes.text:
The *Patience* had been Corin's father's barge, and his grandfather's before that, and it had been moored at the end of Fishbone Walk in the Drowned Quarter for as long as Tamsin could remember.

The Quarter was what had been left of the lower town after the Great Flood eighty years ago. The sea had come up and not gone back. Half the streets were canals now, and the other half were canals at high water, and the people who lived there lived upstairs and kept boats tied to their window-sills. Tamsin had grown up three houses along from the Dasks. She had learned to swim before she learned to read. She still could not walk down Fishbone Walk at night without smelling her mother's kitchen.

The rain had eased by the time she got there, to a fine drifting mist that hung in the lamplight over the water. There was a light in the *Patience*'s cabin, and smoke from the stovepipe, and a small figure sitting on the cabin roof with its knees drawn up and a fishing line over the side.

"He's inside," said the figure. "You're late. He said you'd be late."

"Hello, Wren."

Wren was ten, or eleven, or possibly nine; nobody knew, least of all Wren. She had turned up in the Quarter two winters ago, sleeping under the Fishbone bridge, and Corin had started leaving food for her, and now she slept on the *Patience* most nights and ran messages for anyone who paid her and fished off the roof when no one did. She had a pointed face and very short black hair she cut herself with a knife.

"Caught anything?"

"An eel. Then it got away. Then a boot." Wren pointed at a boot on the roof beside her. "It's a good boot. It's just the one."

Tamsin went down the ladder into the cabin. It was low and warm and smelled of tar and wet wool and fried onions. Corin was at the stove with a pan, and he looked round as she came in, and for a moment his face did something she did not have a word for. Then he grinned.

"You came."

"I said I would."

"You say a lot of things." He pointed the spatula at the bench. "Sit. Eat. Then show me."

She ate. Onions and bread and a piece of smoked fish, and a mug of something hot that had a good deal of rum in it. Wren came down halfway through and ate the rest of the fish out of the pan with her fingers. Then Tamsin took the oilskin packet out of her waistcoat and put it on the table, and the three of them looked at it.

"I didn't show anyone," she said. "But Vane knows. Somebody told him I'd been asking about the *Gannet*, and I don't know who, because the only person I asked was him. And then Mother Agathe knew, three hours later. She asked me about it straight out."

Corin was quiet. Then he said, "Vane told her."

"I think so."

"So they talk."

"The Exchequer and the Guild talk all the time, Corin. That's the whole—" She stopped. "No. You're right. It was too fast. He'd have had to send to her the minute I left his office."

She told him about the register then, the *Gannet* coming in on the twenty-fifth of Rimefall with Bessaly at the helm, stamped by Vane's own hand, and Corin's face went very still.

"That's a lie," he said. "She was on the Teeth by then. I saw her there myself before the twentieth. I saw her mast."

"I know."

"Then why—"

"I don't know." She untied the twine. Her fingers were stiff and it took a long time. Inside the oilskin there was a second layer, waxed cloth, and inside that a letter, three or four sheets folded together into a thick packet and sealed with a great blob of green wax. The seal had been pressed with something that left the shape of a ship's wheel. On the outside, in brown ink that had run a little at the edges where the water had got in after all, it said again: *To the Lamp. By hand.*

"It's wet," Wren said.

"It's damp." Tamsin turned it toward the stove. "If we dry it slow it'll be all right."

"Are we going to open it?" said Wren.

"No," said Tamsin and Corin together.

Corin rubbed his face. "It's not ours. It's for the Lamp. That's what I wanted to tell you this morning." He looked at her. "The old sailors on the Stair, when they talk about the Lamp, they mean the tower. Tidewatch. They mean the old man who keeps the light. Brother Hale."

"The tide-priest?"

"He's kept the tables for forty years. Every tide, high and low, every day, written down. Ruth Bessaly knew him. Everyone who ever crossed the bar knew him." He touched the edge of the letter, very lightly, with one split knuckle. "She knew she was going to drown, Tam. She nailed this under her chart table because she knew. And she wrote it to him."

They dried the letter by the stove, turning it every few minutes like a piece of toast, until the paper was stiff and crackled and the brown ink had stopped spreading. Then Tamsin wrapped it up again in the waxed cloth and put it back inside her waistcoat.

"Wren," Corin said. "Do you know the way to Tidewatch?"

"Course I know the way to Tidewatch."

"Go up there now and find the brother, and tell him that Corin Dask from the *Patience* and a friend want to see him tonight about Ruth Bessaly. Just that. Don't say anything else, not to him and not to anyone you meet on the way. Can you do that?"

Wren held out her hand. Tamsin found a copper in her pocket and put it in it, and Wren looked at the copper and then at her and then put it away somewhere in her clothes and was gone up the ladder without another word.

She came back two hours later, soaked to the skin, with her hair standing up in wet spikes. The brother would see them. He said to come at the night tide, when the light was lit, and to come up the sea stair and not the town stair, and to bring nobody else.

scenes.title: The Lamp
scenes.text:
The sky had cleared by midnight. Tamsin had not seen stars over Quell since the autumn, and there were so many of them, hard and white and close, that she kept stopping on the sea stair to look up until Corin took her arm and made her keep climbing.

Tidewatch stood on the last spur of rock at the mouth of the inner harbour, where the estuary narrowed before it opened out toward the Teeth. It was older than the town. Nobody knew who had built it. It was a round tower of grey stone, a hundred and forty steps from the water to the lamp-room, and the sea stair wound up the outside of it, open to the wind, with an iron rail on the outer side that had rusted through in places so that you had to remember where not to lean. Corin remembered. He went first, slowly, his bad leg dragging a little on every third step, and called back the gaps to her.

The door at the top was open. Inside there was a round room full of the smell of lamp oil and old paper, and a great brass lens behind a screen, turning, throwing its light out through the windows in long slow sweeps over the water. Every few seconds the room went bright and then dim, bright and then dim. Under the lens, at a table covered in books, sat an old man in a brown robe writing by the light of a candle.

"Shut the door," he said, without looking up. "Then come and sit. I'll be a moment. The tide does not wait while I make conversation."

They shut the door and sat on a bench by the wall. Brother Hale wrote for some minutes more, consulting a brass instrument at his elbow that looked something like a clock and something like a compass, and then he blotted the page and closed the book and turned round.

He was older than Tamsin had imagined, very thin, with a long bony face and white hair cut short as a soldier's. His hands were knotted with age and stained black at the fingertips with ink. But his eyes were clear and grey and they went straight to Corin, and then to her, and stayed on her.

"You are the girl from the Exchequer," he said.

Tamsin stared at him. "How do you—"

"The child told me a friend. Corin Dask has only two friends who are not lightermen, and one of them is a tide-priest, and the other one works in a building with a roof." He held out his hand. "Ruth wrote to me. I've been waiting for it. Give it here."

She gave him the letter. He held it to the candle and looked at the seal for a long time without breaking it, and his face, which had been sharp and amused, went slack and old.

"That's her wheel," he said. "That's her own seal. I gave her that ring." Then he broke the wax with his thumbnail and unfolded the sheets and began to read.

Nobody spoke. The great lens turned and the light swept round, bright and dim, bright and dim. Out on the water the tide was making; Tamsin could hear it, a low steady hush against the foot of the tower that was growing louder all the time. Brother Hale read the first sheet and the second, and then he went back and read the first again, and then he read the third and fourth very slowly, with his finger under the lines.

When he had finished he put the sheets down on the table and smoothed them flat.

"Do you want to know what it says?"

"Yes," said Tamsin.

"It's not a kind thing to know."

"I've already been asked about it by the Chief Assessor and by Mother Agathe Sorrel," Tamsin said. "In the same afternoon. I think I'd rather know."

He looked at her for a long moment. Then he nodded, and picked up the first sheet, and read it out to them in a dry level voice, as though it were a tide table.

Ruth Bessaly had sailed for the Salt Guild for twenty-two years. For the last five of them, she wrote, the Guild had been selling ships to the sea. That was what they called it among themselves. A Guild ship would be entered at the Exchequer as carrying salt, outbound, duty paid. Then it would be entered again as lost — lost at the Teeth, lost in a gale off the north coast, lost with all hands — and the Guild would claim the Crown's wreck-rebate on the duty and on the cargo both. A lost ship's cargo was insured by the Crown. That was the old law, from the days when the Margravine wanted salt to keep coming whatever the cost. The rebate on a forty-ton cargo was more than the cargo was worth.

But the ships did not sink. They were never even loaded. The salt went north on other hulls, Guild hulls under false names, and was sold untaxed in the northern markets. The ships that were entered as lost were taken out to the Flats and broken up, or renamed and sent to work somewhere they were not known. Five years. Bessaly had counted eleven ships.

"And the *Gannet*?" said Corin.

Brother Hale turned to the third sheet. "She was to be the twelfth. They told Ruth in the autumn. She was to take the *Gannet* out to the Flats on the second of Rimefall and leave her there, and the *Gannet* would be entered as lost on the Teeth a fortnight later. Ruth refused." He read: "*I told the Mother I would not do it, and she said she understood, and she was very gentle with me, and I am more frightened now than I have ever been at sea. I think they will sell me to the sea with my ship. If you get this, Brother, it will be because they have.*"

The light swept round. Tamsin found that her hands were shaking and she held them together in her lap.

"There's more," Hale said. "There's a reason she wrote to me and not to the Margravine's men. She says this." He turned to the last sheet and read: "*They will enter the Gannet as having come in, after. They always do it so, to make the books balance — an inbound entry to show the cargo was never landed, so the rebate is clean. When they do, look at your tables. They are lazy and they do not look at the tide.*"

He got up, quite quickly for an old man, and went to the shelves on the far wall, where the tide books stood in rows, forty years of them, bound in brown calf with the years stamped in gold on the spines. He took one down and opened it on the table and ran his finger down a column.

"What date is the inbound entry?"

"The twenty-fifth of Rimefall," Tamsin said. "In the morning. It says on the morning flood."

He found the line. He looked at it, and then he turned the book round so that she could see it, and put his finger on the figure.

"Low water at the bar on the twenty-fifth of Rimefall," he said, "was at ten past seven in the morning. A neap tide, and a north wind holding the water off. There was less than three feet over the bar from five o'clock until nearly noon. A sixty-ton salt barge draws seven." He closed the book. "Nothing came into Quell on the morning of the twenty-fifth. Nothing could have. The *Gannet* would have been sitting on the bar with her keel in the sand, in full view of this window. I'd have seen her. I'd have written her down."

Corin let out his breath. "So the register's a lie."

"The register's a lie that can be proved," said Brother Hale, "which is a different and much more dangerous thing." He looked at Tamsin. "You understand that?"

"Yes."

"Edric Vane stamped that entry?"

"He says he did. He says he remembers it. He said Ruth was in a foul temper about the fog."

"There was no fog on the twenty-fifth." Hale almost smiled. "It's in the book. Clear and cold and a north wind. Edric never did look at the weather." He folded the letter up again, carefully, along its old creases. "I'll keep this. It's addressed to me, and this tower has a door that locks, which is more than can be said for a lighter. You will not tell anyone you've been here. Either of you. Go down the sea stair and not the town stair. If anyone asks you where you've been tonight, you were on the *Patience* and you were drunk."

"And then what?" said Tamsin. "We know. You can prove it. And then what?"

Brother Hale looked at the letter in his hands.

"And then I'll think," he said. "I'm an old man, child, and it's past midnight. Let me think."

They went down the sea stair with the wind behind them. Halfway down, Tamsin looked back, and saw the light still turning in the lamp-room, sweeping its long slow arm over the water, and below it, on the town side of the tower, at the foot of the town stair, a man standing very still in the shadow of the wall, with a lantern that was shuttered almost closed.

She said nothing to Corin. She was not sure, afterwards, that she had seen it at all.

scenes.title: What Iska Heard
scenes.text:
Iska Sorrel had learned to listen on the stairs when she was six years old, and she had never yet been caught.

It was a matter of knowing the house. Sorrel House was three hundred years old and every board in it had its own voice, and Iska knew them all: the fourth stair that cracked like a pistol shot, the landing board that sighed, the place outside her mother's door where if you stood on the left you were silent and if you stood on the right you might as well ring a bell. She knew that the door of the Mother's room never quite closed, because the frame had dropped in the Flood year and nobody had ever had it planed. And she knew that if you sat on the seventh stair from the top with your back against the wall, in the dark, you could hear everything said in that room as if you were sitting in it.

She was sitting there now, at a little after one in the morning, with her nightgown tucked under her feet for warmth, because Edric Vane had come to the side door twenty minutes ago and been let in by her mother herself.

That had never happened before. Her mother did not open doors.

"—up the town stair and then round," Vane was saying. He sounded out of breath, and annoyed about it. "Mell's man saw them go up together, the girl and the cripple. They were up there an hour. Then they came down the other side."

"Did they bring anything away?"

"He couldn't see. It was dark."

"It's always dark, Edric. That is why we pay Mell's men, so that they can see in it." Her mother's voice was quite calm. It was the voice she used for bad news about cargo prices. "And the old man has the letter now. Bessaly's letter."

"We don't know there is a letter."

"There is always a letter. There was a letter with Penhallow, five years ago, and you didn't believe me then either. I had the boy fish it out of the dock with a boathook in the end." A pause. The click of rings. "Hale will go to the Margravine's justiciar. Not tomorrow. He'll wait, he's a cautious old creature. He'll want to be sure. He'll go through his books. A week, perhaps."

"Agathe, if Hale has his tables—"

"Then the tower must have a bad night." Very calmly. "Old towers do. Lamp oil, and old paper, and an old man who sleeps in his chair. Mell will see to it. Not yet. When the girl has gone back to her desk and stopped looking over her shoulder."

On the seventh stair Iska put her hand over her own mouth and held it there.

"And the girl?" said Vane.

"The girl's yours. She's your clerk. Frighten her. Take her seal, if you have to. Give her a reason to be quiet that she can live with." The rings again. "And Edric — the second book. I want it out of this house. I don't want it here if the justiciar comes knocking with a warrant. Take it to the Exchequer and put it in the flood vault, where nobody can get at it without your key and the spring tide."

"Tonight?"

"Next spring tide. Four days. Until then it stays in my box, and the key stays round my neck, where it's been for twenty years."

Vane said something Iska didn't catch. Her mother laughed, a dry small sound like a dead leaf.

"I'm sixty-eight years old, Edric. I sleep very soundly. Go home."

Iska went up the stairs before the door opened, on the left side, in the dark, and got into bed with her heart going like a hammer and lay looking at the ceiling. She heard Vane go down, and the side door, and her mother's slow steps along the landing, and the door that never quite closed.

She knew the box. She had known it all her life: a small iron strongbox under her mother's bed, with brass corners and a lock shaped like a scallop shell. She knew the key, too, on its chain, warm from her mother's skin. When she was little she had been allowed to play with it while her mother told her stories, and she remembered the weight of it in her palm, and the way the wards were cut in the shape of waves.

She waited until the bells of the Saltmarket had struck three. Then she got up and went along the landing, on the left side, and pushed the door that never quite closed, and went in.

scenes.title: The Salt Pans
scenes.text:
"She said not to go on my own," Tamsin said. "I'm not on my own."

"That's a lawyer's answer." Corin leaned on the pole and the lighter slid out from under the shadow of the causeway into the open water of the estuary. "You'd make a good Guild mother."

"Take that back."

"I'll take it back if we get home."

It had rained since dawn, a heavy grey rain that flattened the water and blotted out the far shore, and they were both soaked before they had passed the last of the Quarter's chimneys. Tamsin sat in the bow with her shawl over her head and her notebook buttoned inside her coat and watched the Flats come up out of the rain ahead of them: a long low country, neither land nor sea, mile after mile of mud and marsh-grass and shining water, laid out in squares like a chessboard where the Guild had built its salt pans.

The Breme saltworks had been there for two hundred years. The pans were shallow pools walled with clay, a hundred feet on a side, and at the spring tides the Guild let the sea in through sluices and then shut it in and let the sun and wind take the water away and leave the salt behind. In summer the whole Flats glittered white. Now, in Thawmonth, in the rain, it was all grey, grey water in grey pans, and the long low sheds where the salt was stored stood up out of it like the backs of drowned animals.

"Where?" Corin said.

"Bessaly said they break them up on the Flats. You don't break up a ship in a salt pan. You'd need a slip. Somewhere with hard ground."

"There's the old boatyard at Cray's End. Guild's had it shut for years." He pointed with his chin. "There. Past the last sheds."

They tied up at the end of a rotten jetty and walked. The ground was mud with a skin of shingle over it that gave under their boots. Nobody was about. Tamsin had thought there would be saltworkers, but the pans were empty and still in the rain and the only sound was the wind and the sucking of their feet. Corin went slowly. Once his bad leg went into a soft place up to the knee and she had to haul him out by the collar, and they both stood there swearing and laughing in the rain.

The boatyard at Cray's End was a long shed with its seaward end open to a slipway of black timbers. The doors on the land side were chained, but the chain went round a post that had rotted at the base, and Corin lifted the whole post out of the ground and they went in.

It was dark inside, and smelled of tar and wet sawdust and something else, an old cold smell like a church. As her eyes adjusted Tamsin saw that the shed was full of timber, stacked to the roof along both walls: ribs and planks and knees, masts with the rigging still on them, rudders, hatch-covers, a ship's wheel leaning against a post. All of it sorted. All of it neatly stacked and ready to be used again.

And along the back wall, propped one beside the other like gravestones, the nameboards.

She walked down the line of them with her lantern. They were long curved boards from the sterns of ships, carved and painted, most of them faded and some of them freshly gilded. *Kittiwake. Merrow. Sweet Annie. Dorcas Bell. The Honest Woman.* She stopped at that one for a while. *Seaholly. Plover. Constant.* She took out her notebook with wet fingers and wrote them down, one by one, while Corin held the lantern.

Eleven. Bessaly had counted eleven.

There was a twelfth board at the end of the line, newer than the rest, and blank. Someone had planed the old name off it and not yet painted a new one. In the raw wood, if she held the lantern at a slant, she could just see the ghost of the letters where the paint had soaked in. G and a run of letters and a T.

"They were going to bring her here," she said. "They were ready for her."

"And she wouldn't come." Corin's voice was rough. "So they put her on the Teeth instead."

He had picked up something from the floor by the wheel: a small brass bell, green with salt, with a name stamped round the lip. He turned it so she could read it. *Kittiwake*.

"Put it down."

"It's proof."

"It's a bell. Put it down, Corin, we've got the names, that's enough—"

Somebody shouted outside.

They both froze. The shout came again, closer, from the land side, and a dog began to bark. Through a gap in the planking Tamsin saw lanterns coming along the dyke from the sheds, three of them, four, and men behind them, big men in the oilskins and clogs the saltworkers wore.

"The slip," said Corin. "Go."

They went down the slipway at a run into the rain. The tide was coming in. It had been out when they arrived, the mud bare and shining to the edge of the channel, and now there was water over the mud, an inch, two inches, moving in fast across the flats in a long thin silver sheet the way the tide moved on the Flats, faster than a man could walk. They ran through it. Behind them the dog was going mad on the slipway and somebody was shouting *stop, you, stop there*, and a lantern swung out over the water.

They reached the lighter with the water up to their shins. Corin threw her in and fell in after her, and pushed off with the pole, and the channel took them, and the rain closed behind them like a door.

It was not until they were halfway back across the estuary, shaking and soaked and with the Quarter's chimneys coming up out of the rain ahead of them, that she saw he still had the bell. He had it inside his coat. He looked at her, and his chin came up, and he did not say anything, and she did not either.

scenes.title: The Drowned Quarter
scenes.text:
Iska Sorrel found her at the chapel of St Brannoc's that evening, which Tamsin would not have thought was possible, since nobody but the Quarter's own people even knew the chapel was there.

It stood at the far end of Fishbone Walk where the Walk ran out into open water. The Flood had taken its lower half eighty years ago and never given it back, so that now you came to it by boat and climbed in through what had been the clerestory windows, and stood on a gallery above a nave full of black water, with the tops of the pews just showing and the painted saints on the walls up to their chests in the sea. The Quarter's children came here to dare each other to swim the nave. The Quarter's old women came here to pray. Tamsin came here when she wanted to be somewhere nobody from the Exchequer would ever find her, and she had been sitting on the gallery for an hour with her wet notebook drying on her knee when she heard someone climbing in through the window behind her.

"Your messenger," Iska said, "is very expensive."

"Wren?"

"She wanted a silver crown to tell me where you were. I gave her two, to make sure she'd forget me after." Iska sat down on the gallery beside her. She was wearing a plain brown cloak over her Guild black, and her boots were wet to the ankle, and she was carrying a bundle wrapped in sacking under her arm. "I said don't go to the Flats."

"I didn't go alone."

"That's a lawyer's answer."

Tamsin laughed, she couldn't help it, and Iska looked at her as if she had lost her mind.

"Sorry. It's — somebody said that to me this morning." She sobered. "How do you know I went?"

"Because the foreman at Cray's End sent a boy to my mother at noon to say that two people had been in the boatyard, a woman and a man with a lame leg. My mother was very calm about it. My mother is always very calm." Iska looked down at the black water under the gallery. "She calls it selling ships to the sea. Did you know that? She's done it for five years. She used to say it at dinner, when I was younger, as a joke. *We've sold another one to the sea, Iska.* I thought she meant they'd sunk."

"Some of them did," Tamsin said.

"Yes." Iska did not look up. "I know that now."

She put the bundle on Tamsin's knees. It was heavy and square. Tamsin unwrapped the sacking and found a ledger, an ordinary account book bound in plain brown board, with nothing written on the cover.

"It's the second book," said Iska. "The true one. Every ship they've sold, every rebate, who was paid and how much. My mother has kept it since the start. She keeps everything. She thinks if she writes a thing down it belongs to her." She drew a breath. "Edric Vane's name is in it on every page. So is Mell's. Captain Mell, of the watch."

Tamsin opened it. The pages were close-written in a small, upright, old-fashioned hand, with sums in the margins. She turned to the back and found the last entry: *Gannet. To the Teeth. 2 Rimefall. R.B. not to be paid*.

She closed the book. Her hands were not quite steady.

"How did you get it?"

"I took it out of the box under her bed while she was asleep. Last night. Three in the morning." Iska's mouth twisted. "She sleeps very soundly. She told him so."

"Told who?"

So Iska told her. About Edric Vane at the side door, and the seventh stair, and the tower that must have a bad night. About Mell's man at the foot of the town stair. About Vane's orders: frighten the girl, take her seal. About the flood vault and the spring tide in four days, three now.

"She said not yet," Iska said. "She said she'd wait until you'd stopped looking over your shoulder. But that was before I took the book. When she finds it's gone, she won't wait."

"Has she found it?"

"I don't know. I put a book of psalms in the box in its place. The same size." Iska almost smiled. "She doesn't read psalms."

Tamsin sat with the ledger on her knees, and the black water of the drowned nave below her, and the painted saints looking up at her out of the sea.

"I have to warn him," she said. "Brother Hale."

"Yes."

"Tonight. I have to go up there tonight."

"They'll be watching the tower," Iska said. "Mell's men. Both stairs. If you go up there tonight they'll know you've been warned, and then they'll know someone warned you, and there are only so many people who could have." She looked at Tamsin, finally. "Send the child in the morning. Nobody watches a mudlark. And Tamsin — keep that book somewhere they won't look. Not the Exchequer. Not your rooms."

"Where, then?"

Iska stood up. She pulled her brown cloak round her, over the Guild black.

"Somewhere you'd never go," she said. "I'd put it in a church."

scenes.title: Wrecker
scenes.text:
They came for Corin a little after midnight.

Tamsin was on the *Patience* when they did. She had not meant to be; she had meant to go home to her rooms on Lantern Stair and sleep, but she had walked back along Fishbone Walk from the chapel in the dark with nothing in her arms, the ledger left behind her wrapped in oilskin and wedged up inside the hollow of the painted St Brannoc's lifted hand where only a swimmer could reach it, and when she came to the barge there had been a light in the cabin and she had gone down.

Corin was mending a net. He did not ask where she had been. He gave her the rest of the rum and she drank it and told him about Iska and the ledger, and he listened without saying anything, and when she had finished he said, "Good," and went back to his net. Wren was asleep on the bench under a pile of coats.

The first Tamsin knew of them was the barge tilting. Somebody heavy had stepped onto the deck. Then another. Then the hatch was pulled back and a lantern was shoved down into the cabin, and behind it a face she knew: red and square, with a sandy moustache, under the tall leather cap of the Harbour Watch.

"Corin Dask," said Captain Oszkar Mell. "Up you come."

Corin put down the net. "What for?"

"Wrecking." Mell came down the ladder. He was a big man and the cabin was suddenly very small. Two more watchmen came down behind him. "You were seen on the wreck of the *Gannet* two nights ago, taking goods out of her. The Guild's laid a complaint." He looked round the cabin, and saw Tamsin, and his eyes rested on her a moment longer than they needed to. "Evening, miss."

"He didn't take anything," Tamsin said. "He went out to look, that's all, that's not a crime—"

"Is it not." Mell looked at Corin's coat on its hook. He put his hand into the pocket and brought out the little green bell. *Kittiwake*. "What's this, then?"

"That's not from the *Gannet*," Tamsin said, and then stopped, because Mell was smiling, and she understood a second too late what she had just told him.

"No? Where's it from, then, miss?"

Nobody said anything. On the bench Wren had woken and was lying very still under the coats with her eyes open.

"Bring him," said Mell.

Corin went without a fight. He stood up and put his coat on and went up the ladder with a watchman in front and one behind, and on the deck he turned and looked back down at her through the hatch.

"Feed the child," he said. "There's fish in the box."

Then they took him along the Walk toward the Tidegate Gaol, with the lanterns bobbing, and Tamsin stood on the deck of the *Patience* in the dark and watched them until they went round the corner, and Wren came and stood beside her and put a cold hand in hers and did not say anything at all.

scenes.title: Vane's Office
scenes.text:
She sent Wren up to Tidewatch at first light with a message she made her repeat three times — *the tower is to have a bad night, leave it, come down* — and then she washed her face in the canal and went up the hill to the Exchequer and asked to see the Chief Assessor.

He kept her waiting an hour. She sat on the bench outside the glass door and watched him through it, writing at his desk by the fire with his back to her, and the forty clerks in the Ledger Hall bent over their desks and did not look at her, any of them, in a way that told her they all knew she was there.

When he called her in, he did not get up.

"Shut the door, Miss Orrey."

She shut it. It was warm in his office. She had never been in it before. There was a carpet, and a second chair by the fire, and a picture of the Margravine over the mantel looking down her long nose at the room. His desk was very tidy. There was a silver inkstand, and a blotter, and his seal on its stand, the anchor in a ring.

"Captain Mell tells me," Vane said, "that a friend of yours was taken up last night for wrecking."

"Corin Dask didn't wreck anything, sir."

"He had goods from a wrecked ship in his coat. In front of a witness. In front of two witnesses, I'm told." He took off his spectacles and looked at her. "Do you know what the penalty is for wrecking, Miss Orrey? In Quell, under the old law?"

She did. Everyone in the Quarter did. They had hanged a man on the Tidegate for it when she was twelve and left him there through two tides.

"He found that bell at Cray's End," she said. "In a boatyard the Guild's had shut for years. Along with the nameboards of eleven ships that the Exchequer entered as lost at sea." Her voice was shaking; she let it. "I have the names. I can give you the names, sir, and you can look them up in the register, and you'll find your stamp on every one of them."

Vane did not move. He sat looking at her with his spectacles in his hand.

"And the *Gannet*, sir. You stamped her inbound on the morning of the twenty-fifth of Rimefall. On a neap tide, with a north wind. There was three feet of water over the bar. She draws seven. You said Ruth Bessaly was in a temper about the fog, but there wasn't any fog." She made herself say it. "It's in the tide books, sir. At Tidewatch."

For a long moment there was no sound but the fire.

Then Vane put his spectacles down on the blotter, very precisely, and opened the drawer of his desk, and took out a sheet of paper already written on and signed.

"This is an order suspending you from the service of the Exchequer," he said, "for conduct unbecoming. Pending inquiry. You'll leave your seal with me." He held out his hand.

She looked at it. Every assessor had a seal. Hers was small and brass, on a cord round her neck, with her number cut in it — two hundred and six — and nothing else; a junior's seal, good for countersigning counts and nothing more. She had been so proud of it the day they gave it to her that she had slept with it in her hand.

"Your seal, Miss Orrey."

She took the cord over her head and put the seal in his palm. He closed his fingers on it and put it in the drawer and shut the drawer.

"Now listen to me," he said. "Because I am going to say this once, and I am saying it because I liked your Mr Faraday, and he liked you. Corin Dask is in the Tidegate. Whether he stays there until the assize, and what happens to him at the assize, is a matter on which Captain Mell is willing to be guided by this office. Do you understand me?"

"Yes," said Tamsin.

"The old man in the tower is very old. Old men have accidents. You will not go up there again." He put his spectacles back on. "And you have nothing. You have a list of names on wet paper, and a tide book in a tower, and a lighterman in gaol for theft. You have no ledger, and no letter, and as of this morning, no seal. Go home, Miss Orrey. Stay there. In a month, perhaps, we'll talk about your coming back."

She went. She went out through the glass door and down the length of the Ledger Hall between the two rows of high desks, with forty clerks not looking at her, and down the stairs, and past Hobb the porter in his box, who smelled of cloves and said *Morning, miss* as if nothing had happened, and out into the street.

He had said no ledger. He had said no letter. He did not know that Iska had the book — that it was gone. And he thought Hale still had the letter, or he would not have said *old men have accidents* in that voice.

She stood in the street and the wind went through her. She had told him about the tide books. She had stood in his warm office and told him, in so many words, exactly what the old man in the tower could prove.

Wren came round the corner at a run.

"He won't come," she said, before Tamsin could speak. "I told him. Three times, like you said. He just said thank you and gave me this and said give it you." She held out a book bound in brown calf, with a year stamped on the spine in gold. "He says it's the one that matters. He says he'll keep the letter where it is. He says the tower's stood eight hundred years and it's not going to fall down for Agathe Sorrel."

scenes.title: Fire at Tidewatch
scenes.text:
The bell of the Saltmarket began to ring at a little before two in the morning, and Tamsin was already awake.

She had not undressed. She had sat up all evening in her rooms on Lantern Stair, with the tide book on the table in front of her and Wren asleep in her bed, listening to the town go quiet. She had gone to the window a hundred times. From her window you could see, over the roofs, the top of Tidewatch and its slow sweeping light, and every time she looked the light was there, turning, bright and dim, bright and dim, and she had begun to think that perhaps it would be all right, that perhaps Agathe would wait after all, that perhaps Iska had been wrong.

Then she looked, and the light was the wrong colour. Orange, not white. And it was not turning.

She was down the stairs and in the street before the bell started. Wren was behind her; she had not woken Wren, but Wren was there, barefoot, running. The streets were full of people coming out of doors in their nightclothes, pointing. Everyone in Quell knew what the light meant. If the light at Tidewatch went out there would be ships on the Teeth by morning.

They ran down through the Saltmarket and along the harbour front to the foot of the tower. A crowd had gathered on the quay at the bottom of the town stair, and the watch were there, holding them back, and above them the top of the tower was burning. Fire came out of the lamp-room windows in sheets. Glass was falling, bright, tinkling on the stones.

"Is he out?" Tamsin was shouting at the nearest watchman. "The brother, is he out, has anyone gone up—"

"Stand back, miss. Nobody's going up there."

She did not stand back. She went round the foot of the tower to the sea side, where there was no crowd, and up the sea stair with the rusted rail, and Wren came after her and she did not have breath to send her back.

She had climbed it two nights ago with Corin calling out the gaps. She remembered them now: the seventeenth step, the fifty-second, the long stretch above the ninetieth where the rail was gone altogether and the wind came straight off the sea. The smoke was coming down the stair from above, thick and choking, and she pulled her shawl over her mouth and kept her other hand on the wall and climbed.

The door at the top was open. Inside it was all smoke and roaring and a terrible light. The great lens had cracked across and fallen from its stand. The shelves along the far wall were burning, forty years of tide books burning, the gold on their spines running in little bright streams. And on the floor by the table, half under it, as if he had tried to get under it to the air, was Brother Hale.

She got her hands under his arms and pulled. He was so light. He was so light it was like pulling a coat. She got him out onto the stair, into the wind, and the smoke rolled out over them and away, and she knelt on the step with his head in her lap.

He was alive. His face was black with soot and his eyebrows were gone and one of his hands was burned so badly she could not look at it. But his eyes opened, grey and clear, and found her.

"Exchequer," he said.

"Don't talk."

"Must." He coughed, a terrible tearing cough. "Mell. Two men. Came up the town stair. Oil." He coughed again. "I should have — gone down. You said. I'm a stubborn — old—"

"Brother, please, they're coming, they'll get you down—"

"Listen." His good hand moved at his chest, under the robe. She helped him, and found a cord round his neck, and on it a key: brass, long and heavy, its bow worked in the shape of a wave. "Flood vault. Under the Exchequer. Two keys. Chief Assessor has one. Tower has the other. Old law. So that no — one man — can—" He could not finish. He pushed the key at her. "Spring tide. Day after tomorrow. The water lifts the weight. Then the door will open."

She took it. It was warm from him.

"The letter," she said. "Ruth's letter. Is it—"

He looked past her, at the doorway, at the fire.

"Burned," he said. "I'm sorry. Kept it where it was. Stubborn." His eyes came back to her. "You have the book. The tide book. That's what — matters. Numbers don't — lie. Ruth knew." He smiled, or tried to. "Lazy. Never looked at the tide."

Then his eyes went past her again, up, at the stars over the sea, and stayed there.

She did not know how long she knelt there. A long time. The watch came up the sea stair eventually, with buckets and a ladder, and somebody took him out of her lap, and somebody else put a blanket round her, and she let them. On the quay below, the crowd was quiet now. The fire in the lamp-room had burned down to a red glow. Out on the water there was no light at all, and she thought of the Teeth in the dark, and the ships that would be out there tonight not knowing.

Wren was sitting on the step below her with her knees drawn up. When the watch had gone down with the brother, she reached into the front of her shirt and took something out and held it up.

It was a small brass seal on a cord, with a number cut in it. Two hundred and six.

"Hobb lets me run messages up to the Ledger Hall," Wren said. "The glass man always leaves his drawer unlocked when he goes out for his dinner." She put the seal into Tamsin's hand and closed Tamsin's fingers over it, the way Tamsin had once closed Wren's fingers over a copper. "I thought you'd want it back."

scenes.title: Under the Exchequer
scenes.text:
The spring tide came at dawn on the seventh of Thawmonth, and Tamsin Orrey went down to meet it with a dead man's key round her neck and her own seal back on its cord beside it.

She had not slept. She had spent the day after the fire in her rooms with the shutters closed, while the town talked about the old priest who had knocked over his lamp, and the watch put up a notice on the Saltmarket cross offering a reward for information about the lighterman Dask's accomplices in the matter of the *Gannet*, and Wren went in and out with bread and news. Nobody came for her. That frightened her more than if they had. It meant Vane was content to wait. It meant he thought she had nothing.

The flood vault was older than the Exchequer. The building had been put up on top of it two hundred years ago, but the vault itself had been cut into the rock of the hill by whoever had built Tidewatch, for the same reason and in the same stone. It was where the Crown's copies were kept. Every register entry made in Quell was copied twice, once into the green book on the lectern and once onto loose sheets that went down into the vault each quarter, sealed, to be sent to the Margravine's treasury at Hesk at the year's end. The vault could be opened only at the spring tides, when the sea came up the old culvert under the hill and lifted the great iron counterweight that held the door. Two keys. One for the Exchequer and one for the tower. So that no one man could.

Hobb was in his box when she came in by the side door at half past five. He looked at her, and at the seal on its cord, two hundred and six, and she saw him remember that she had been suspended, and then she saw him decide that it was half past five in the morning and that he had not been told.

"Early, miss."

"The count," she said. "Spring tide."

"So it is." He went back to his newspaper.

The stair down to the vault was behind a door at the back of the archive room, and the door was not locked, because there was no need. At the bottom of the stair there was a short passage cut in the rock, wet and cold and smelling of the sea, and at the end of the passage there was the vault door: a slab of black iron eight feet high, with two keyholes in it side by side, and above it, on a great chain running up into the dark, the counterweight.

She could hear the water. It was below her somewhere, in the rock, booming and sucking in the culvert. As she stood there it grew louder. Then the chain above the door gave a groan and a shudder, and the counterweight began, very slowly, to rise.

She put Hale's key into the right-hand keyhole. It turned as if it had been oiled yesterday.

The left-hand one was Vane's. She had known that, and she had come anyway, because she had thought — she had not let herself think it clearly, but she had thought it — that Vane would come. That he had to bring the second book down and put it in the vault on this tide, as Agathe had told him to, and that he did not yet know the book was gone. That he would come down the stair with his key, and find her.

She heard his step on the stair behind her.

"Miss Orrey," said Edric Vane.

He was in his greatcoat with a lantern, and he was alone, and he had a bundle under his arm wrapped in oilskin, the same size and shape as the book Iska had brought to the chapel. Tamsin looked at it, and could not help herself; she laughed.

"What?" He sounded, for the first time since she had known him, entirely at a loss. "What is it?"

"It's psalms," she said. "Sir. Unwrap it. It's a book of psalms."

He looked down at the bundle. He did not unwrap it. She watched him understand, the way she had watched him understand nothing, for three years, through the glass door; and she watched him look at the key in the right-hand lock, the wave-shaped bow, and understand that too.

"Hale," he said.

"Hale's dead. You know he is. You sent Mell."

"I didn't send anybody." His voice cracked on it. "I didn't — that was her. I told her not to. I told her the tower was too much." He put the lantern down on the floor. His hands were shaking. "You don't understand. Twenty years, Tamsin. She had me twenty years ago. A gambling debt and a letter I shouldn't have written. Twenty years, and everything I've stamped since, she's had a hand on it."

"Open the door, sir."

"Why should I?"

"Because the Crown's copies are in there. And if your stamp on the copies says what the register says, then it's your word against the tide book, and you might come out of it. But if it doesn't — if somebody along the way didn't bother copying a lie onto a sheet that was going to sit in the dark for a year—" She took a breath. "Then it's only her, isn't it. You can say she made you. You can say it to the justiciar."

He stood looking at her for a long time. Behind the door the sea boomed in the rock, and the counterweight hung at the top of its chain.

Then he took his key out of his waistcoat pocket and put it in the left-hand lock and turned it.

The door swung inward on a breath of cold salt air. Inside was a small round chamber lined with iron shelves, and on the shelves, in sealed bundles with their quarters written on the outside in red ink, the Crown's copies. Hundreds of them. She found the quarter she wanted in a minute and broke the seal with her thumbnail, the way she had seen Brother Hale break Ruth Bessaly's wax, and leafed through the sheets by Vane's lantern.

*Gannet. Breme. Master R. Bessaly. Outbound 2 Rimefall.*

And after that, nothing. No inbound entry. Whoever had copied that quarter's sheets had copied the true register, before the lie had been written into it — or had not been told.

She held the sheet up. Vane looked at it. He sat down very slowly on the wet stone step, with his back against the wall and his useless bundle of psalms on his knees.

"Faraday copied that quarter," he said. "He was always slow. He was always weeks behind."

"Yes, sir," said Tamsin. "He told me once. The only way to read a register is all the way to the end."

The water came up through the floor of the passage behind them, an inch, two inches, and the counterweight began to groan on its chain. She took the sheets, and took his arm, and got him up the stair before the door swung shut.

scenes.title: The Tide Court
scenes.text:
The Tide Court sat at noon in the old hall under Saltmarket Cross, which had been a fish market before it was a court and still smelled faintly of it in wet weather. It was not wet weather. It was the first bright day since autumn, a hard blue sky and a wind off the sea that sent the gulls sideways and rattled every shutter in the town, and the hall was full to the doors.

Tamsin had not known so many people would come. She stood at the front, at the long table where the witnesses stood, with the things she had brought laid out in front of her: the Crown's copy sheets for the quarter, with Faraday's slow careful hand on them; a brown calf tide book with the year stamped on its spine in gold; and the ledger, the second book, with the sacking still on it and a smell of the drowned chapel, which Iska had swum the nave for that morning at low water because Tamsin could not have reached it alone. Iska stood beside her now. She had dried her hair, but she had not changed out of her Guild black, and she held herself very straight.

Justiciar Pell sat on the bench under the Margravine's arms. He was a thin, dry, middle-aged man who had come down from Hesk the year before and was said to dislike Quell, its smell, its tides and its Guild, in roughly that order. He had read the ledger already. He had sat with it for two hours that morning in the robing room, and he had come out looking like a man who had bitten something bad.

Mother Agathe Sorrel sat at the other table in her high-backed chair, which four Guild men had carried down from Sorrel House, with a rug over her knees. She did not look at her daughter.

It took less time than Tamsin had expected. It was the tide book that did it. Pell had it opened at the twenty-fifth of Rimefall and laid beside the register, the green book with the anchor in a ring stamped against the *Gannet*'s inbound entry, and he looked from one to the other several times, and then he looked at Edric Vane.

Vane was standing at the side of the hall between two watchmen. He looked very old. He had not slept either, Tamsin thought; he had been up all night in a room in the Tidegate with a clerk of the justiciar's, and his gold spectacles were folded in his breast pocket and he did not take them out.

"Chief Assessor," Pell said. "Was the *Gannet* in Quell on the twenty-fifth of Rimefall?"

"No, my lord."

"Then why does your stamp say that she was?"

Vane looked at Agathe Sorrel. Everyone in the hall looked at Agathe Sorrel.

"Because Mother Agathe told me to put it there," Vane said. "My lord. As she told me to put the others."

Agathe did not move. The rings on her hands lay still in her lap. When Pell asked her whether she had anything to say she turned her good eye on him, slowly, the way she had turned it on Tamsin in the room above Guild Row, and said, "I keep a ledger, my lord. Like any merchant. So does the sea," and nothing more, then or afterward.

Captain Mell was not in the hall. He had been seen at dawn on the north road with two horses and a heavy saddlebag, and the justiciar's men had gone after him, and in the end they would bring him back. But that was later. That was another week.

Corin came out of the Tidegate at four o'clock, when the justiciar's order reached it. Tamsin was waiting on the quay outside with Wren, and he came out blinking in the sunlight, thinner, with a week's beard and his split knuckles healed to pink, and he stood on the top step with his weight on his good leg and looked at her.

"Did you feed the child?" he said.

"She fed me, mostly."

"I did," said Wren.

They walked back along the harbour to the Quarter, the three of them, slowly, because of his leg. The wind had dropped and the tide was going out, the great spring ebb that would leave the whole estuary bare to the Teeth before dark, and the light lay gold on the mud. On the far side of the water, on the spur of rock at the harbour mouth, Tidewatch stood black and roofless against the sky. There were men on it already with ladders and a block and tackle. The Margravine had sent word: there would be a new light by the next dark of the moon.

"Who'll keep it?" said Corin. "There's nobody who knows the tables."

Tamsin thought of the brown calf book on the table in the Tide Court, and the forty years of others that had burned, and the old man writing by candlelight with the great lens turning over his head.

"Someone will learn," she said.

They came to Fishbone Walk, and the *Patience*, and there was smoke from the stovepipe, because Iska Sorrel was sitting on the cabin roof with her Guild black hitched up to her knees, fishing, badly, off the side. She looked up as they came along the Walk.

"I had nowhere else to go," she said. "Is that all right?"

Corin looked at her, and at Tamsin, and at Wren, and at the boot that was still sitting on the cabin roof beside Iska, the good boot, the one that had come up on Wren's line a week ago.

"There's fish in the box," he said.
